common_name: Wild Ceylon Cardamom (Greater Cardamom, Long Cardamom)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in constantly moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade; this wild-type variety is largely collected from rainforest understory rather than field-grown, so plants establish best under a closed forest canopy that mimics its native habitat. Suited only to zone 10-12.

directions: This is the wild, indigenous form of cardamom found in the rainforests of southwestern Sri Lanka, distinguished from the cultivated Malabar and Mysore types (var. minor) by its notably taller stature, larger elongated seed pods, and inflorescences that stand more erect above the foliage rather than trailing along the ground. It is only rarely brought into cultivation today, valued mostly by collectors and gene banks preserving cardamom's genetic diversity, since commercial growers favor the higher-yielding cultivated types. Give it the same deep, humid shade, constant soil moisture, and rich organic mulch that true cardamom requires, and expect a slower, more forest-like clump that takes several years to flower. Because seed-grown wild stock is variable and difficult to source, propagation is almost always by division of established rhizome clumps.
sources: PROSEA - Plant Resources of South East Asia
Sri Lanka Export Development Board - Ceylon Cardamom

planting.note: Divide established clumps in warm weather and plant in rich, well-drained soil (pH 5-6.8) in partial shade beneath open tree canopy; Java cardamom dislikes both full sun and drought and needs consistently high humidity to thrive.

directions: Native to the lower hills of western Java and now cultivated across Sumatra and the Moluccas, this compact ginger-family relative forms clumps of upright, dark green reed-like pseudostems that stay smaller and tidier than true cardamom or black cardamom. The small, round, pale-skinned pods that form at the base of the plant are known as kapulaga in Indonesia, where they season rendang, gulai, and other spiced braises and are steeped into jamu herbal tonics. It prefers dappled shade under a tree canopy, steady warmth between roughly 50-95F, high humidity, and frequent rainfall, resenting both dry spells and direct sun. Because seed-grown plants are slow and inconsistent, most growers propagate by dividing rhizome clumps, and newly divided plants take a few years to reach flowering and bearing size.
sources: PROSEA - Plant Resources of South East Asia

common_name: Chinese Cucumber (Tian Hua Fen, Gua Lou)

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat for 24 hours before direct sowing once soil has warmed, and provide a tall trellis or arbor; plant both male and female vines since this species is dioecious and needs a pollinator partner to set fruit. Hardy to zone 8-9, where the tuberous root often survives winter and resprouts in spring.

directions: Unlike its tropical cousins snake gourd and pointed gourd, Chinese cucumber is a temperate-climate vine native to China, Korea, and Japan that dies back to a large tuberous root each winter and can survive outdoors as far north as zone 8. Its claim to fame is not the bitter, inedible fruit but the plant's use in traditional Chinese medicine: the dried root (tian hua fen), the ripe fruit rind and pulp (gua lou), and the seeds (gua lou ren) are all harvested as distinct medicinal preparations, the root typically dug in autumn once vines are several years established. The vine itself is also a striking ornamental for a sunny trellis or arbor, producing intricately lace-fringed white flowers that open at dusk and are followed by round to oval fruit that ripens from green to bright orange-red. Grow it in full sun on rich, well-drained soil with a sturdy support, and be patient, since the root needs two to three seasons to bulk up to a size worth harvesting.
sources: USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has fully warmed, giving the sprawling vines a large trellis or open ground space; this is a released Indian research-station cultivar bred specifically for high flesh yield rather than long storage.

directions: Kashi Dhawal is an ash gourd cultivar released by ICAR's Indian Institute of Vegetable Research in Varanasi, selected from a local landrace for its oblong fruit, thick white flesh, and unusually high flesh-to-rind ratio. Vines are long and vigorous, reaching well over 20 feet, and fruits mature in about 120 days into large, greenish-white, waxy-coated gourds commonly weighing 11-12 pounds. Its dense, high-recovery flesh makes it the preferred type for making petha, the popular Indian candied ash gourd sweet, though it cooks and stores like any other winter melon in curries and soups. Grow it exactly as you would standard winter melon, in full sun on deeply worked, fertile, moisture-retentive soil with a heavy-duty trellis or generous ground space to support the long vines and heavy fruit.
sources: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi - Ash Gourd Varieties
